text: The other twenty-four, one line each. Sorting first. Merge sort halves, sorts each half and merges in linear time: n log n always, stable, with linear extra memory. Python's sort builds on it. Heapsort guarantees n log n in constant extra space, but is less cache-friendly than quicksort. It suits tight memory. A stable sort keeps ties in order. Sort by first name, then stable-sort by last, and the two Hoppers stay in first-name order. In place means constant extra memory, or log n of stack: quicksort, with random pivots. Out of place grows with the input: merge sort. The Master Theorem solves divide-and-conquer recurrences by comparing the work of combining with the number of smallest pieces. For merge sort they tie, so n log n. Recursion fits trees, but every call takes a stack frame, and Python stops at a thousand. A loop with an explicit stack avoids that. Divide and conquer splits into independent subproblems, like merge sort. Dynamic programming reuses the answers of overlapping ones. Memoization recurses and caches, top-down. Tabulation fills a table bottom-up. Naive Fibonacci of thirty makes two point seven million calls; memoized, fifty-nine. Know coin change, longest common subsequence, knapsack, edit distance and word break: each teaches a way to define the state. Greedy takes the best-looking step, safe only when local choices provably add up. To make six from coins of one, three and four, it takes three coins. Two threes do it. Backtracking builds a candidate step by step and drops a branch the moment it can't succeed: N-Queens, Sudoku, permutations.
